<p class="sardine-eyebrow">DERAILED / MARINE LIFE / AN AQUARIUM DETOUR</p>

# Who is leading the sardines?

<p class="sardine-lede">My aunt suspected there was a leader. The sardines declined to comment.</p>

## 01 / One ray. A lot of sardines.

I visited **Aquamarine Fukushima** with my relatives and found myself completely mesmerized by the sardines in the big Kuroshio tank.

Hundreds of little silver fish, swimming together, turning together, somehow never bumping into one another. I could have watched them for hours.

Then a **カラスエイ** (*pelagic stingray*) glided through. The **マイワシ** (*Japanese sardines*) scattered, only to regroup and carry on as if nothing had happened.

My aunt had a theory:

<blockquote class="story-quote">
  <p>“There must be a good leader.”</p>
  <footer>— My aunt, at the aquarium</footer>
</blockquote>

I love this answer. It makes perfect sense from the outside. If a whole crowd moves in sync, surely someone must be calling the shots?

But... **which fish?** And how would everyone else get the memo in time?

## 02 / Meet the actual fish

Before making cartoon sardines swim around a browser, I wanted to know a little more about the two animals that started this whole detour.

```{=html}
<div class="species-pair">
  <div class="species-card">
    <span class="species-label">THE SCHOOL</span>
    <h3>マイワシ <em>True sardine</em></h3>
    <p class="species-latin">Sardinops melanostictus</p>
    <p>They gather near the sea surface, from coastal waters to offshore. Look closely: the row of dark spots along their sides has earned them the Japanese nickname <strong>七つ星</strong>—“Seven Stars.” They also migrate north and south with the seasons.</p>
    <p>Why swim in a school? Possible advantages include safety in numbers, spotting danger sooner, and reproduction. There isn't just one explanation.</p>
    <a href="https://www.aquamarine.or.jp/animals/true-sardine/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Aquamarine's マイワシ profile ↗</a>
  </div>
  <div class="species-card">
    <span class="species-label">THE SURPRISE VISITOR</span>
    <h3>カラスエイ <em>Pelagic stingray</em></h3>
    <p class="species-latin">Pteroplatytrygon violacea</p>
    <p>A dark-backed ray that swims through open ocean water rather than spending most of its life along the seabed. It moves with those broad, wing-like fins.</p>
    <p>Here's a fun twist: when feeding, it can actually <strong>turn belly-up</strong> and use its fins to help bring food toward its mouth. Our earlier upside-down sardine suddenly has some competition.</p>
    <a href="https://www.aquamarine.or.jp/animals/pelagic-stingray/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Aquamarine's カラスエイ profile ↗</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

Aquamarine Fukushima's Kuroshio tank recreates a little of the ocean's eat-or-be-eaten world, bringing predators and prey together.  Pelagic stingrays do eat sardines, but the one I watched wasn't visibly hunting. It simply glided through, and the school parted around it, then flowed back together.

What fascinated me wasn't the predator. It was how effortlessly hundreds of little fish responded together.

## 03 / Okay, but who is in charge?

I couldn't bring the aquarium home. So I drew one sardine, taught it to swim, and made 47 more. Then I gave each fish a way to react to its neighbours.

No conductor. No group chat. No extremely organized fish manager.

<div class="sardine-intro">ONE FISH → MANY FISH → A FEW SIMPLE RULES → WHAT HAPPENS?</div>

## 04 / Try taking the leader away

Here's the experiment I'd love to show my aunt:

1. **Watch the school** for a bit. Nobody has been assigned as the leader.
2. Switch from **Schooling** to **Independent**. Same fish, same tank. They're still swimming, but they aren't paying attention to one another. What happens?
3. Switch **Schooling** back on. Do you notice the difference?
4. Turn down **alignment**, **cohesion**, or **separation**, one at a time. Which rule seems to matter most?

Change the number of sardines, make them smaller, or follow the dotted path of one individual. That little highlighted fish is just the one we're watching—not the captain.

You can also click the tank to set a shared destination. That's fun, but remember: giving everyone a common target is different from asking how a group coordinates without one. For that question, keep **Free swim** selected.

## 05 / Three rules. No boss.

The simulation is inspired by *Boids*, a model introduced by computer graphics researcher Craig Reynolds in 1987. It starts with three surprisingly ordinary ideas:

- **Separation:** “Excuse me, you're a bit close.”
- **Alignment:** “Oh, we're going that way?”
- **Cohesion:** “Hey, where did everyone go?”

Each fish responds to the neighbours it can 'see' in our simplified model. None of them knows the shape of the whole school. Yet a recognizable group can take shape anyway.

That kind of larger pattern arising from lots of small interactions has a name: **emergence**.

The code is much simpler than a real sardine. Real fish have eyes, senses, three-dimensional water to navigate, currents, and much more going on. This experiment isn't proof that real マイワシ behave according to exactly these rules. It's a way to test whether a leader is *necessary* for coordinated-looking movement.

## 06 / And what about the カラスエイ?

We haven't put a ray in our simulated tank. **Not yet.**

That's actually the part I'm most curious about. What if a big ray-shaped obstacle moved through the school? Would each sardine reacting locally be enough to make the whole school open up around it?

There are other questions too. Were the fish avoiding the ray itself, the movement of nearby sardines, or a combination of cues? Watching them through the glass didn't tell me—and this first model can't tell me either.

But now I have an experiment to try. All because my aunt made one little comment at the aquarium.

<p class="sardine-outro">“There must be a good leader.”<br>Maybe. Or maybe the fish just need good neighbours.</p>

<p class="sardine-source"><strong>The real animals:</strong> <a href="https://www.aquamarine.or.jp/animals/true-sardine/">マイワシ</a>, <a href="https://www.aquamarine.or.jp/animals/pelagic-stingray/">カラスエイ</a>, and Aquamarine Fukushima's <a href="https://www.aquamarine.or.jp/exhibitions/sea-of-current-rip/">Kuroshio tank</a>. <strong>The model:</strong> inspired by <a href="https://www.red3d.com/cwr/papers/1987/boids.html">Craig Reynolds' 1987 Boids work</a>; a two-dimensional illustration, not a reconstruction of the aquarium encounter. <a href="https://github.com/chichacha/derailed/issues/16">DERAILED #16</a> · <a href="https://github.com/chichacha/psychic-pento-guacamole/issues/115">Gomasu #115</a>.</p>
